title: First marriage to Lucille Forby in California
summary: In 1931 he married a chorus girl, Lucille Forby, despite warnings from Eddie Anderson; it lasted only months.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: I tell you what. We should touch on -- we've got time.
We should touch on your life and your marriages. We didn't get too much into that.
I happen to know -- I was there in Cab Calloway's band when you met a lovely lady in Memphis, Tennessee.
Well, my first marriage, I married a chorus girl --
-- out in California. I was young. I was dumb. I didn't know. And this girl was a real fast girl. She was way faster than I would ever think about being.
And she was a beautiful girl, and I
And I was going with another girl at the time out there, too, a chorus girl. And her name was Johnnie Mae Johnson. She became a dancing -- a dancing team, Smiles and Smiles.
I liked her. Her name was Lucille Forby.
And Eddie Anderson, who later became Rochester, told me, he said, 'Quent, you don't want her. She's not the right kind of girl for you.'
How did you meet Eddie Anderson?

Eddie Anderson was working in Sebastian's Cotton Club, in the show. He and Johnny Taylor had a pantomime act together and it was funny. This was a funny thing, one of the funniest things you ever saw in your life, that they did. They used to fall all down the steps and slide way out on the floor, you know. But it was all pantomime.

And so Eddie Anderson told me, he said, "You --" -- you know, I told him to tend to his own business. And I went on like a fool. The girl -- it was like a thing where she said -- she took me home, you know, and we made love -- she said, "Let's get married." I said, "Okay." She said, "I bet you won't." I said, "I bet I will." And we went on and applied for the license, like fools.

And we had an afternoon wedding out to her house, had an Episcopalian minister and everything, and the pillows to kneel on. And the Chez Norman Grill was a wonderful restaurant at that time and we had an afternoon dinner at the Chez Norman Grill, --
-- you know, that the gang at the Cotton Club had given us, you know, and it was really beautiful.
But that marriage didn't last. She stayed in California and she met me, she came to meet me in Detroit and I found out then that this girl was a playgirl.
She wasn't for marriage. So, you know, so we stayed together and that was like in June she came -- let me see. September she came to me. And December we were separated.

That's right. And so I didn't get married anymore. So I started to hanging out with all the chicks that I could so I could find out about women. All kinds of women I hung out with and I asked a million questions. And I wasn't going to get tied down with anyone, you see? That was September '32 -- no, '31. I didn't see her no more until when I came to New York and joined Don Redman, and I looked at her and I told her, 'Uh-uh, no, no. Uh-uh.'
But I was man enough -- she needed a coat, she didn't have no winter coat. I bought her a winter coat that winter.
And she was living with a guy. And so I gave her a bag so that she could go on back to Philadelphia. She was working in a club there, because she was a singer, too. And that was the end of that.
